_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version. Concepts are the catalog's w01 slugs (classes, responsibilities, strategy-pattern); the catalog has no slug for tell, don't ask, so it is taught under responsibilities. Title from the Workshop bible v1.0.1 (the catalog's lld title is Parking lot). Of the bible's three wrong ideas, the shared gate object is left out; the branch in the count and the subclass per level are the bad options.
title: The Car Park That Lied
setting: a hospital's staff car park at the 19:30 shift change

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The hospital car park board I programmed said level 2 had 14 free bays. At the same minute, the barrier told a nurse the car park was full.

blocks.text: My great-aunt, Winifrith Torvaine, built coin-operated machines and clockwork figures for sixty years. In her last ten she also wrote programs, the lists of steps a computer follows, for local shops. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. I'm Odgerel. I program on night shifts and finish her machines in the evenings. Each still has its paper work order tied on with string.

One is the barrier program for the staff car park at Abbotsmere Hospital: five levels, 60 bays on each. A sensor, a small detector over each bay, tells the program when a vehicle arrives or leaves. At the entrance a driver taps a staff pass. First the gate looks up what that person drives. Then it picks an empty bay that fits, shows its number and lifts the barrier. A board over the entrance shows free car bays per level.

blocks.title: WORK ORDER 41. Abbotsmere Hospital, staff car park.
items: Level 1, bays 51 to 60 become motorbike bays.
Level 2, bays 45 to 60 become charging bays, where an electric car plugs in. Electric cars only.
The board shows free car bays per level, and free motorbike bays.
Search order: by day, the top level down. From 19:00, nearest the lifts first, for staff walking out in the dark.

blocks.text: Winifrith wrote the program as classes. A class is a pattern for one kind of thing in code, like a blank form; each real thing made from it is an object. There is a Gate class, a Level class and a Bay class; each of the 300 bays is a Bay object.

Her program knew one kind of bay, so I added branches for the new kinds. A branch is a fork in the code: if this is true, do that. Here is the gate's method, a set of steps a class carries out. It tries levels in the search order, and each empty bay in number order:

Gate.pickBay(vehicle)
  for each level, then each empty bay:
    if bay is motorbike: fits = vehicle is motorbike
    if bay is charging:  fits = vehicle is electric
    if bay is ordinary:  fits = vehicle is not motorbike
    if fits: send it there, stop
  none fits: show CAR PARK FULL
Each level also counts its own free bays for the board. I gave that count a branch for motorbikes, because the board shows them apart. Every other empty bay counts as a car bay:

Level.freeBays()
  for each empty bay:
    if bay is motorbike: motorbikes + 1
    else: cars + 1

It went live on Thursday at noon, when the chargers were switched on. All afternoon there was room, and nobody was turned away. At the 19:30 shift change, the night shift arrives before the day shift leaves.
At 19:40 Cliodhna, a nurse on the night shift, tapped her pass. Here is the board above her, then the gate's last lines: time, pass number, vehicle, and the bay it gave:

board 19:40  L1 0  L2 14  L3 0  L4 0  L5 0  motorbikes 3
19:33:48  pass 0817  electric  level 2 bay 46
19:35:52  pass 2208  petrol    level 4 bay 58
19:40:14  pass 3390  petrol    CAR PARK FULL

Her car runs on petrol. She pressed the intercom to the security desk. Proinsias, the guard on duty, lifted the barrier by hand; she parked in a charging bay on level 2 and reached her ward 9 minutes after the 19:45 handover began. Proinsias rang Domitila, who rang me at 20:05.
Fourteen bays free. Car park full. Both answers came from my program.
Beside this program, Winifrith's notebook has one line in pencil: *Only the slot may judge a coin.* Domitila wants it fixed before tomorrow's 19:30. What should I change?

blocks.label: level2_at_1940_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: Level 2 at 19:40, redrawn. Cliodhna's petrol car taps in at 19:40:14. Gate.pickBay, whose charging branch says electric only, finds no bay and the barrier shows CAR PARK FULL. Bays 1 to 44 on level 2 are ordinary with 0 empty; bays 45 to 60 are charging bays with 14 empty. Level.freeBays counts every bay that is not a motorbike bay as a car bay, gets 14, and the entrance board shows level 2: 14.

blocks.caption: I redrew level 2 at 19:40 from the sensors. Bays 1 to 44 are ordinary and all taken. Bays 45 to 60 are charging bays; the two electric cars tonight took 45 and 46, so 14 are empty. The gate asks whether a petrol car fits each empty bay and finds none. The level's count only asks whether a bay is a motorbike bay, so it sends 14 to the board.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Put your two listings side by side and pick one bay: level 2, bay 50, empty at 19:40. Ask the gate's method whether a petrol car fits it. Then ask the level's count whether it is a free car bay. Write both answers down. What a class is in charge of knowing or doing is called its responsibility. So: which class in your program is responsible for knowing who may park in bay 50, and how many classes answer that question? Then think about the next kind of bay the hospital adds, and read Winifrith's line again. In her coin machines, what decided whether a coin was a coin?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The work order also has the two search orders, and I wrote them as one branch on the clock inside pickBay: before 19:00 the top level down, from 19:00 the lifts first. Programmers call a set of swappable ways of doing one job, each its own small object behind the same call, a strategy. Domitila says the porters want a third order for snow nights, with level 5, the open roof, closed.

comments.author: u/one_more_branch_gottlieb
comments.text: You did it right for motorbikes and forgot charging bays. That's the whole bug: one missing branch in the count. Add it, check that level 2 reads 0 on the board tonight, and go to bed. Rebuilding classes the night before a shift change is how you ship three new bugs.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Sveinbjorn, who looks after the hospital's computers, would go one step further: give each level a subclass for its mix of bays. A subclass is a class built on another one that changes only what differs. Level 2 would be a ChargingLevel and level 1 a MotorbikeLevel, each with its own count.

comments.author: u/one_table_ragnheidur
comments.text: Your rules are scattered over two classes. Put them in one table instead: a grid with a row for each kind of bay, a column for each kind of vehicle, and yes or no in each square. The gate and the level both look the answer up there. One place to read, one place to change.

reply.prompt: Tomorrow's 19:30 shift change will fill the car park again. What should Odgerel change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add a branch for charging bays to the level's count, to match the gate's.
options.part2: I added one line to Level.freeBays: a charging bay counts for electric cars, not for cars. On the bench, Thursday's nine arrivals now end with the board at 0 on every level when the 19:40 car is turned away, so a driver could see from the road that the car park was full. On Wednesday 21 October Domitila asked for a night rule: from 19:00 to 07:00 any car may use a charging bay, and the board should show them free. Sveinbjorn made the change in Level.freeBays, the count the board uses, and didn't know the gate kept its own copy. On Thursday 22 October, during the shift change, the board showed free bays on level 2 while the barrier told a porter the car park was full. Proinsias let him in by hand, and he was late onto his ward. On the bench, the night rule made in the count only gives the same lie: 14 on the board, the 19:40 car turned away.
options.senior: The branch fixes tonight's count and leaves the program with two copies of one fact: which vehicles may use which bay. Copies drift. Every new kind of bay and every change to a rule must now be made in the gate and in the count, by whoever makes it, who may not know there are two. The board lies again the first time someone edits one copy. Give the fact one home and make everything else ask it.

options.text: Give each level a subclass for its mix of bays, each with its own count.
options.part2: I made MotorbikeLevel, for level 1, and ChargingLevel, for level 2, subclasses of Level, each with its own count; levels 3 to 5 stayed plain Levels. On the bench, Thursday's arrivals end with the board at 0 on every level, which is right. In November the electricians turned bays 45 to 50 on level 1 into charging bays too. Level 1 was a MotorbikeLevel, whose count still called every bay that isn't a motorbike bay a car bay. On the bench, with those six bays added, the two electric cars take level 1 bays 45 and 46, the board says 4 free on level 1, and the 19:40 car is turned away. At the first shift change after the new chargers, level 1 showed free bays while the barrier turned a radiographer away; Proinsias let her in by hand. Sveinbjorn has started a MotorbikeChargingLevel.
options.senior: Subclasses split the count by level, but the fact still lives outside the bays, now in more places: the gate, MotorbikeLevel and ChargingLevel. A level is a mix of bays, and mixes change, so every new mix needs a new subclass or a copy of an old one. This is inheritance used to vary what a thing holds, a common trap. The kind of bay is what varies, so the rule belongs on the bay.

options.text: Let each bay say which vehicles fit it; make the search order a strategy.
options.part2: I gave each kind of bay its own small class, OrdinaryBay, ChargingBay and MotorbikeBay, each with one method, fits(vehicle). Level.freeBays now counts the empty bays where fits(a petrol car) is true, and the gate asks each bay the same question, in an order handed to it by a strategy: NearestLifts from 19:00, FromTheTop by day. On the bench, Thursday's arrivals end with the board at 0 on every level when the 19:40 car is turned away: the car park really was full, and now the board says so. On Wednesday 21 October Domitila asked for the night rule, any car in a charging bay from 19:00 to 07:00. I changed ChargingBay.fits, one place, and the gate and the board changed together. On the bench the 19:40 car now goes to level 2, bay 50, nobody is turned away, and the board reads 10 on level 2 and 3 on level 4, as the gate does. Two electric-car drivers asked Domitila why petrol cars sat in charging bays at night; that is Domitila's rule, and it stays. The snow-night order is one new strategy class.
options.senior: Give each fact one owner. A bay's kind decides who may park in it, so the bay answers fits(vehicle), and the gate and the level ask it instead of reading its kind and deciding again: tell, don't ask. A new kind of bay is then one new class, and a rule change is one edit that every reader sees. The search order is a separate decision that changes for its own reasons (by day, at night, in snow), so it is a strategy handed to the gate, not a branch on the clock inside it.

options.text: Keep one shared table of which vehicles fit which bays, for gate and levels.
options.part2: I wrote one table, a row for each kind of bay and a column for each kind of vehicle, and made the gate and Level.freeBays both read it. On the bench, Thursday's arrivals end with the board at 0 on every level, which is right. On Wednesday 21 October Domitila asked for the night rule. A yes or no in a square can't say "from 19:00 to 07:00", so I added a night column and taught both readers to check the clock: three places to edit, the table, the gate and the count. I changed all three, and on the bench the 19:40 car goes to level 2, bay 50, and the board agrees. Nobody was turned away at the next shift change. Then Sveinbjorn asked where the snow-night order should go, and the table had no square for that either.
options.senior: A shared table gives the facts one home, which fixes tonight, and it is a fair choice when the rules really are a grid of yes and no. But the rules still sit away from the bays, and anything that isn't a plain yes or no, such as a rule that depends on the time, ends up as code in every reader. Each change then touches the table and every reader, and a reader someone forgets brings the lie back. Put the rule on the bay and the readers only ask.

sim.title: Run the shift change through the barrier program
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying Thursday 15 October 2026 from 19:00, before the first arrival. Each level has bays 1 to 60: level 1 has motorbike bays 51 to 60, level 2 has charging bays 45 to 60, and every other bay is ordinary. At 19:00, five bays fit a petrol car (level 2 bays 23 and 41, level 4 bays 37, 52 and 58), all 16 charging bays are empty and 4 motorbike bays are free. Nine vehicles arrive by 19:40:14. The gate tries the levels in the search order and each empty bay in number order, and sends each vehicle to the first bay that fits. The board shows each level's free car bays as the design counts them. Change the design, the search order (nearest the lifts, or from the top) and a later change: the night rule (any car in a charging bay from 19:00 to 07:00) made everywhere it lives or in the count only, or six charging bays added on level 1.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step four times and watch level 2's board figure as the first electric car takes bay 45. Play the rest: 14 on the board, CAR PARK FULL at the barrier. Try each design; all but the first are right tonight. Then add the night rule in the count only, with the branch and then with each bay answering. Add the six charging bays on level 1 with the subclass. Last, switch the search order to from the top and count who is turned away.

explain.oneLine: Neither class was broken on its own. The gate and the level's count each kept their own copy of who may park in which bay, the copies disagreed about charging bays, and the board showed the count's 14 while the gate, rightly, found no bay for a petrol car.

steps.title: Two classes, one fact.
steps.text: First, Cliodhna tapped her pass, and Gate.pickBay tried every empty bay in the search order. Apart from 3 motorbike bays, the only empty bays left were charging bays 47 to 60 on level 2, and the gate's charging branch said: electric cars only. With no ordinary bay empty anywhere, it showed CAR PARK FULL. Meanwhile Level.freeBays, run for the board, went through the same 14 empty bays and asked a different question: is it a motorbike bay? No, so each one counted as a car bay. Both answers came from code that did exactly what it said. The fact "who may use a charging bay" lived in two classes, and only one of them had been told.

steps.title: Why never before, and why 19:40.
steps.text: Before the work order every bay was the same kind, so the two classes asked the same question and could not disagree. From noon on Thursday the board over-counted level 2 by every empty charging bay, 16 of them at 19:00, but there was room elsewhere, so nobody noticed. The lie only matters once the ordinary bays run out. At the 19:30 shift change both shifts' cars are in; the last ordinary bay went at 19:35:52, and the next petrol car met the difference.

steps.title: Responsibilities: give each fact one owner.
steps.text: A class's responsibility is what it is in charge of knowing or doing. "Can this vehicle use this bay?" is a fact about the bay, so the bay should answer it: OrdinaryBay fits petrol and electric cars, ChargingBay fits electric cars, MotorbikeBay fits motorbikes. The gate and the level then ask each bay fits(vehicle) instead of reading its kind and deciding for themselves. That habit is called tell, don't ask: tell an object what you need, rather than asking for its data and acting on it. It is what Winifrith's line means. In a coin machine only the slot judges a coin, and the counter and the change tube trust its answer. Here the bay is the slot. In SOLID terms (s5e05), each bay class now has one reason to change: its own rule.

steps.title: Choosing a bay is a strategy.
steps.text: The gate makes a second, separate decision: in what order to try the bays. As built, it was a branch on the clock inside pickBay. The strategy pattern (s5e06) turns each way of doing one job into its own class behind the same call. First, each order becomes a small class with one method that lists the bays in order: NearestLifts and FromTheTop. Second, the gate is handed whichever one applies and takes the first empty bay that fits. Third, a new order, such as Domitila's snow nights with the roof closed, is one new class, and the gate does not change. The order matters: replay Thursday from the top and the 19:21 electric car takes ordinary bay 58 on level 4, so two petrol cars are turned away instead of one. What can go wrong: something must pick the right strategy at 19:00, so that choice belongs in one place too.

steps.title: The fix, step by step.
steps.text: First, write OrdinaryBay, ChargingBay and MotorbikeBay, each with fits(vehicle). Second, change Level.freeBays to count the empty bays where fits(a petrol car) is true, and add a figure for electric cars the same way. Third, change pickBay to ask the strategy for bays in order and take the first empty one whose fits(vehicle) is true. Fourth, delete every branch that checks a bay's kind outside the bay classes, and search the code for any you missed. What can go wrong: a new reader, such as a report or a phone app, that checks the kind itself brings a second copy back.

diagram.aria: The fix. A NearestLifts strategy hands the gate the order to try bays from 19:00. Gate.pickBay sends a vehicle to the first empty bay that fits. The entrance board asks Level.freeBays, which counts the empty bays that fit a petrol car. Both the gate and the level ask the bay classes: OrdinaryBay fits petrol and electric cars, ChargingBay fits electric cars, MotorbikeBay fits motorbikes. Every bay answers for itself.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow. Each kind of bay answers fits(vehicle) for itself; the gate and the level ask OrdinaryBay and MotorbikeBay the same way as the ChargingBay shown. The gate takes bays in the order the strategy gives it and sends a vehicle to the first empty one that fits. Level.freeBays counts the empty bays that fit a petrol car, and the board shows that. Both ask the same bays the same question, so at 19:40 the board reads 0 on level 2 when the gate finds nothing.

fix.title: The fix: each bay answers fits(vehicle); the search order is a strategy
fix.text: Move the rule onto the bays: OrdinaryBay, ChargingBay and MotorbikeBay each answer fits(vehicle). Make Level.freeBays count the empty bays that fit a petrol car (and, as a second figure, an electric car), and make Gate.pickBay take the first empty bay that fits, in the order a strategy object gives it: NearestLifts from 19:00, FromTheTop by day. Delete every other check of a bay's kind. A new kind of bay is then a new class, a rule change is one edit, and a new search order is a new strategy.

limits: A bay can only answer for what it knows. A rule that depends on something outside the bay, such as the time of day or a driver's badge, has to reach the bay as an input, fits(vehicle, time), and every caller must pass it the same way.

Tell, don't ask is a guide, not a law. Martin Fowler writes that he doesn't use it himself and prefers the wider aim of keeping data and behaviour together; a report that lists every bay's kind still has to ask.

One place to change a rule makes it easy to change, not right. Under the night rule, petrol cars in charging bays at night can leave an electric car that arrives late with nowhere to charge; that is a choice for Domitila, not the code.

Good
Bad
rows: Branches in the gate, the older rule in the count (as built)
A small change; the gate is right.
Two copies of one fact: the board said 14 while the gate said full.
A charging branch added to the count
Still two copies; the night rule made in one of them brought the same lie back.
A subclass per level's mix of bays
More copies, one per mix; six charging bays on level 1 made the board lie about level 1.
One home for facts that are plain yes or no.
The rules sit far from the bays; a rule with a time in it means editing the table and both readers: 3 places.
Each bay answers fits(); the order is a strategy
One owner per fact; the night rule is 1 edit; a new order is a new class.
More small classes; a rule that needs outside facts must be passed in.

explain.seniorTake: Ask of every fact in a design: which class owns it? If the answer is "two of them", you have found the next bug, and it will show itself the first time someone changes one copy. Put each rule on the object whose data decides it, and make other code ask that object rather than read its data and decide again. Keep decisions that change for their own reasons, such as the search order by day, at night and in snow, apart as strategies. An interviewer who asks for a parking lot is looking for exactly this: spot types that answer for themselves, a level that counts by asking, and an assignment rule you can swap.

realWorld.title: Design Patterns, 1994: strategy's intent
realWorld.text: A pattern catalogue that credits Design Patterns (Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides) gives strategy's intent as "Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable." And: "Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it." NearestLifts and FromTheTop are such a family; the gate is the client.

realWorld.title: When the catalogue says strategy fits
realWorld.text: Among the situations the same page lists: "a class defines many behaviors, which appear as multiple conditional statements in its operations." The as-built pickBay, with its branch on the clock, is one.

realWorld.title: Martin Fowler, 2013: Tell-Don't-Ask
realWorld.text: Fowler's bliki entry says Tell-Don't-Ask "reminds us that rather than asking an object for data and acting on that data, we should instead tell an object what to do." It adds: "This encourages to move behavior into an object to go with the data."

realWorld.title: Fowler's own caveat
realWorld.text: In the same entry: "But personally, I don't use tell-dont-ask." He calls it "a stepping stone towards co-locating behavior and data", which is the aim here: the bay's rule sits with the bay's kind.

realWorld.title: Don't repeat yourself
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article states the principle as "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system" and says it "has been formulated by Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas in their book The Pragmatic Programmer." Who may park in a charging bay was one piece of knowledge with two representations.

asked: How would you add a new kind of parking spot without touching the rest of the system?
What is the strategy pattern, and when would you use it?
interview.answer: Start with the objects and what each is responsible for. A ParkingLot has Levels; a Level has Spots; a Vehicle has a kind; an entrance Gate assigns spots, and a display shows free spots. Put the rule "can this vehicle use me?" on the spot: each spot type has fits(vehicle), so a compact, a motorbike, an electric-charging or an accessible spot answers for itself. A Level counts free spots by asking each spot, and the gate assigns by asking each spot, so the display and the gate cannot disagree. Adding a spot type is a new class, with no edits to the gate or the level. The order of assignment, such as nearest the lifts, fill from the top or nearest an exit, is a strategy: an interface with one method that returns candidate spots in order, one class per rule, handed to the gate and chosen by time of day or by settings. Strategy fits whenever one job has several interchangeable ways of being done and the choice changes for its own reasons; it replaces a chain of if-else on a mode. Name tell, don't ask and don't repeat yourself as the reasons. Then raise the follow-ups: two gates assigning the same spot at once, and keeping spot state through a restart.

The minutes when the outgoing nurse tells the incoming one about each patient. On Cliodhna's ward it began at 19:45, and she arrived 9 minutes after it began.

A bay for any car, petrol or electric.
A bay with a charger an electric car plugs into. At Abbotsmere: level 2, bays 45 to 60, electric cars only, switched on at noon on Thursday 15 October.
A small bay for a motorbike. At Abbotsmere: level 1, bays 51 to 60.
A small detector over each bay that tells the program when a vehicle arrives or leaves, like a doorbell for one space.

A speaker and button at the barrier that rings the hospital's security desk.
The list of steps a computer follows. Winifrith wrote hers in the same notebooks as her clockwork.

A set of steps a class can carry out, such as pickBay() or freeBays().

The gate's method: try the levels in the search order and each empty bay in number order, and send the vehicle to the first that fits; if none fits, show CAR PARK FULL.

What a class is in charge of knowing or doing. Giving each fact one responsible class keeps two classes from disagreeing about it.

Five design principles gathered by Robert C. Martin (s5e05). The first, single responsibility, says a class should have one reason to change.

Odgerel's workbench: the sim, which replays Thursday's nine arrivals through whichever design you pick.
How many places in the code must change to bring in the night rule: 2 as built, with a branch or with subclasses, 3 with a shared table, 1 when each bay answers.

atWork: Look for one fact answered in two places. Common ones: a price worked out in the basket and again on the invoice; "can this order be cancelled?" checked by the web page and again by the server, with different rules; "is this user an admin?" decided in two services. Read-only access to the code is enough. Search for the same check on a type or status field, such as kind == "charging", in more than one class. Each is a board that can lie: it agrees until someone changes one copy. Move the rule onto the object that owns the data, give it a method such as fits() or canCancel(), and make every other place call it. For a choice that varies on its own, such as a pricing or assignment rule by time of day, use a strategy object instead of a branch on the clock.

recall.prompt: A food delivery app has a Restaurant class and a SearchPage class. The restaurant refuses orders outside its opening hours and while its kitchen has pressed Pause. The search page shows an "open now" badge from its own check of the opening hours. On a busy Friday evening, a restaurant on Pause shows "open now" while every order to it is refused. What is wrong with the design, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The rule "can this restaurant take orders?" lives in two classes, and the copies disagree
Give the rule one owner: the restaurant answers it through one method
The search page asks the restaurant instead of checking its data itself: tell, don't ask

recall.model: The rule "can this restaurant take orders right now?" lives in two places: the restaurant's own check, with opening hours and Pause, and a second copy in SearchPage that knows only the opening hours. The copies disagree the moment the rule grows, so the badge lies. Give the rule one owner: a method on the restaurant, canAcceptOrders(), responsible for hours, Pause and anything added later. Then the search page asks the restaurant through that method instead of checking its opening hours itself: tell, don't ask. Delete the page's copy, and any other, so a new rule is one change that every screen shows.

recall.prompt: Level 2 has 44 ordinary bays, all taken, and 16 charging bays, of which 14 are empty. The gate lets only electric cars into charging bays. Level.freeBays counts every empty bay that isn't a motorbike bay as a car bay. A petrol car taps in. What does the board show for level 2, and what does the barrier do?
options: The board shows 0, and the barrier shows CAR PARK FULL
The board shows 14, and the barrier shows CAR PARK FULL
The board shows 14, and the barrier sends the car to a charging bay
The board shows 16, and the barrier sends the car to a charging bay
recall.why: Level.freeBays never asks who may use a bay; it only checks for motorbike bays, so the 14 empty charging bays count as car bays. The gate's own branch says electric only, so it finds nothing for a petrol car. Two classes, two answers.

recall.prompt: Domitila wants a third search order for snow nights: never send cars to level 5, the open roof, and otherwise nearest the lifts first. In the as-built program the order is a branch on the clock inside Gate.pickBay. How would you add the snow order so the gate's code doesn't change, and what is the pattern called?

keyIdeas.idea: Each order becomes its own class behind the same method: the strategy pattern
The gate is handed the chosen order and just uses it; which order applies is picked in one place outside it
The snow order is a new class, and nothing else in the gate or the bays changes

recall.model: Make each search order its own small class with one method that lists the bays in order: NearestLifts, FromTheTop, and a new SnowNight that skips level 5 and otherwise goes nearest the lifts first. They are interchangeable behind the same call, which is the strategy pattern. The gate is handed whichever strategy applies tonight, chosen in one place by the clock or by Domitila's snow switch, and simply takes the first empty bay that fits in the order it is given. Adding snow nights is one new class, with no change to the gate's code or to the bays.

recall.prompt: After the fix, which line in Level.freeBays follows tell, don't ask?
recall.why: It tells the bay what it needs to know, whether a petrol car fits, and lets the bay decide by its own rule. Checking bay.kind, or looking the kind up in a grid of rules, makes the level decide again from the bay's data. Asking the gate puts the rule in the gate, far from the bays.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Every bay answers fits() now, Domitila's change for nights went in as one edit, and the board and the barrier have agreed every evening since. This month Sveinbjorn wrote a phone app for staff that shows free bays before they leave home. It fetches every bay's kind and whether it is empty, and counts as a car bay every empty bay that isn't a motorbike bay. On Thursday 10 December at 07:20, at the morning shift change, the app said level 2 had 9 free. The board said 0, and the barrier turned two cars away.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the app say 9 when the board says 0, why did nobody notice until the morning, and how should Sveinbjorn's app get its numbers?

keyIdeas.idea: The app made its own copy of the rule, the old one from the as-built count, instead of asking the bays
From 19:00 to 07:00 the night rule lets any car use a charging bay, so the copy happened to be right; after 07:00 charging bays are electric only again
The app asks: it gets Level.freeBays, which asks each bay fits(a petrol car), rather than reading kinds

coldCase.model: It's the same mistake in a third place. The app fetched each bay's kind and decided for itself, with its own copy of the old rule: every empty bay that isn't a motorbike bay is a car bay. From 19:00 to 07:00 the night rule lets any car use a charging bay, so at night the copy happened to be right and nobody noticed. After 07:00 charging bays are electric only again, so at 07:20 the app counted level 2's 9 empty charging bays as free while the bays themselves said no. Don't let the app read kinds. Give it what the board gets: Level.freeBays, which asks each empty bay fits(a petrol car), so the app asks rather than decides: tell, don't ask. Then the app, the board and the barrier share one rule.
